\f0\b\fs36 \cf0 \strokec2 3. Scope and Non-Implementation Boundary\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa240\partightenfactor0

\f1\b0\fs24 \cf0 This handoff covers the Commercial branch\'92s approved production-facing requirements: prompt/report behaviour expectations, output rules, guardrails, display-verification needs, live-QA scenarios, non-regression protections and residual limitations.\
It does not cover implementation mechanism, code, schema edits, backend changes, UI design, prompt edits, data-flow changes, score recalculation, scoring-field changes, weighting changes, caps, blockers, verdict thresholds or role-fit bounds.\
Actual implementation planning must decide how to apply the approved Commercial requirements inside production prompts, report behaviour, validation, display labels and QA workflows. Live-output QA must wait until implemented revised Commercial outputs or current relevant Commercial reports are available.\
The following must remain preserved: the six-field model, Commercial weights, server-side recomputation, Step 1 / Step 2 locked pipeline, report schema, public JSON structure, safety/material/accessibility scrubs, UK terminology, timestamp limits and the Musical Theatre acting + song stabilised anchor.\
\pard\pardeftab720\partightenfactor0
\cf3 \strokec3 \
\pard\pardeftab720\sa298\partightenfactor0

\f0\b\fs36 \cf0 \strokec2 4. Commercial Production-Readiness Summary\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa240\partightenfactor0

\f1\b0\fs24 \cf0 Commercial production-facing improvements should clarify that the 
\f2\fs26 acting
\f1\fs24  field means Commercial presence / naturalism only when grounded in observable Commercial behaviour: copy communication, task-calibrated tone, camera relationship, addressee logic, believable scale, product / brand / situation context where supplied, and evidence visible in the tape.\
Commercial must not be treated as theatre acting or generic screen acting. Direct-to-camera, off-camera-reader / scene-style, no-dialogue and voiceover-style contexts require distinct handling. UGC/social-style, presenter-led product and corporate/industrial contexts remain limitations unless the task or brief supplies enough context.\
Commercial outputs must block no-brief invention: no unsupported brand, product, buyer, target audience, campaign world, casting fit or \'93commercial look\'94 claims. Technical and audio evidence should support assessability and reliability; poor sight, sound or framing should narrow confidence before becoming performance criticism. Domestic capture and simple setups can be acceptable; production polish, expensive equipment, paid readers, paid editing or studio quality must not be treated as Commercial merit.\
Reader access, upload burden, file admin, deadlines, slate details and turnaround are process-only unless they affect explicit brief compliance. Live-room capacities such as direction response, callback readiness and campaign-pressure flexibility must not be inferred from a finished tape.\
Accessibility-safe Commercial handling must treat access needs, disability, visual impairment, Deaf/disabled access, hearing difference, speech difference, accent, gender-diverse voice, mobility difference, convalescence and adaptation as fairness / process / assessability contexts, not deficits.\
\pard\pardeftab720\partightenfactor0
\cf3 \strokec3 \
\pard\pardeftab720\sa298\partightenfactor0

\f0\b\fs36 \cf0 \strokec2 13. Implementation-Planning Readiness Decision\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa240\partightenfactor0

\fs24 \cf0 Ready for Commercial implementation planning with explicit limitations.
\f1\b0 \
Rationale: The Commercial branch is complete through synthesis, audit, revision, final audit and output-specificity mapping. The approved Commercial changes are suitable for later production planning as wording, prompt/report-behaviour, evidence-standard, claim-scope, guardrail and QA requirements. They do not require or authorise score-field, weight, schema, backend, pipeline, cap, blocker, verdict-threshold or role-fit changes.\
No Commercial revision blocker remains. The key unresolved items are live-output and display-layer verification gaps: no live Commercial reports or JSONs were supplied, frontend labels and comparison-page behaviour are unverified, and renderer/export timestamp parity remains untested.\
What can move forward: cross-branch implementation planning can include the Commercial production-facing requirements, exclusion rules, generic-phrase replacements, display verification checklist and COMMERCIAL-OS-T01\'96T31 regression pack.\
What must remain as limitation: UGC/social, presenter-led product and corporate/industrial subtype coverage; conditional voiceover support; partly inferential anti-marketability / anti-appearance evidence; and broad access detail for accent, speech difference and gender-diverse voice.\
Live Commercial examples are required before production release sign-off.\
\pard\pardeftab720\partightenfactor0
\cf3 \strokec3 \
\pard\pardeftab720\sa298\partightenfactor0

\f0\b\fs36 \cf0 \strokec2 14. Reusable Handoff Pack for Cross-Branch Implementation Planning\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa240\partightenfactor0

\f1\b0\fs24 \cf0 Commercial is complete through Output Specificity / Non-Regression Test Mapping and is ready to enter cross-branch implementation planning with explicit limitations. The branch evidence base spans COMMERCIAL-S001\'96S030 and produced COMMERCIAL-SYN-F01\'96F24, COMMERCIAL-AUDIT-I01\'96I17, COMMERCIAL-AUDIT-R01\'96R21, COMMERCIAL-REV-C01\'96C21, COMMERCIAL-REV-S01\'96S21, COMMERCIAL-FINAL-D01\'96D02 and COMMERCIAL-OS-R01\'96R21 / T01\'96T31 / I01\'96I15.\
The production-facing Commercial requirement is to make the existing Commercial type more specific inside the current six-field architecture. The 
\f2\fs26 acting
\f1\fs24  field remains unchanged but should be interpreted in Commercial as observable presence / naturalism: copy communication, grounded task-calibrated tone, camera relationship, addressee logic, believable scale and product / brand / situation grounding where supplied. Commercial must not become theatre acting, generic screen acting, voiceover, UGC or presenting by default.\
Commercial reports must require behavioural anchors in headline, category notes, strengths, improvements, fix-first, timestamps and next-take advice. Generic phrases such as \'93natural\'94, \'93confident\'94, \'93strong presence\'94, \'93relatable\'94, \'93authentic\'94, \'93marketable\'94, \'93bookable\'94, \'93commercial look\'94 or \'93good camera work\'94 must be replaced by observable evidence. Tone, copy, product, brand and audience claims require supplied or observable context. No-brief reports must not invent brand, product, buyer, target audience, campaign world or casting fit.\
The main guardrails are assessability before judgement, simple capture over polish, reader/admin/deadline/process-only boundaries, no live-room overclaims, accessibility-safe non-deficit language and anti-marketability / anti-appearance exclusions. Technical and audio issues should narrow reliability before becoming Commercial-performance criticism. professional_presentation must stay limited to assessability, explicit brief compliance and safe process.\
Display verification remains essential after implementation: category labels, acting-as-presence semantics, omission of irrelevant Vocal labels, comparison-page parity, timestamp count/order/specificity, feedback reliability and professional_presentation wording must be checked. No live Commercial outputs were supplied, so live Commercial QA remains pending. Required regression tests are COMMERCIAL-OS-T01\'96T31.\
Non-regression protections: preserve six score fields, Commercial weights, server-side recomputation, Step 1 / Step 2 locked pipeline, caps, blockers, verdict thresholds, role-fit bounds, report schema, public JSON, safety scrubs, maximum note limits and the MT acting + song anchor.\
COMMERCIAL-IMPLEMENTATION-HANDOFF complete. Ready for cross-branch implementation planning.\

\f2\b\fs36 \cf0 \strokec2 9. Topic-by-Topic Audit Summary\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa280\partightenfactor0

\fs28 \cf0 Commercial distinctiveness from theatre acting\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa240\partightenfactor0

\f0\b0\fs24 \cf0 Current baseline status: partial.\uc0\u8232 Key risk: theatre-style acting feedback may replace Commercial copy/camera/tone evidence.\u8232 Recommendation IDs: R01.\u8232 Revision scope note: add Commercial-not-theatre boundary.\u8232 Watch item: keep Acting branch protected.\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa280\partightenfactor0

\f2\b\fs28 \cf0 Commercial distinctiveness from generic screen acting\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa240\partightenfactor0

\f0\b0\fs24 \cf0 Current baseline status: partial.\uc0\u8232 Key risk: \'93screen naturalism\'94 becomes too generic and ignores copy/product/campaign context.\u8232 Recommendation IDs: R01, R02, R04.\u8232 Revision scope note: distinguish Commercial screen evidence from general screen acting.\u8232 Watch item: do not overbuild weak subtypes.\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa280\partightenfactor0

\f2\b\fs28 \cf0 acting-as-presence/naturalism field semantics\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa240\partightenfactor0

\f0\b0\fs24 \cf0 Current baseline status: partial.\uc0\u8232 Key risk: 
\f3\fs26 acting
\f0\fs24  score rewards vague presence.\uc0\u8232 Recommendation IDs: R02.\u8232 Revision scope note: clarify 
\f3\fs26 acting
\f0\fs24  as Commercial naturalism, copy communication, camera relationship and tone evidence.\uc0\u8232 Watch item: no score-field or weighting change.\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa280\partightenfactor0

\f2\b\fs28 \cf0 Generic \'93natural / confident / presence\'94 suppression\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa240\partightenfactor0

\f0\b0\fs24 \cf0 Current baseline status: partial.\uc0\u8232 Key risk: generic praise without evidence.\u8232 Recommendation IDs: R03, R20.\u8232 Revision scope note: require observable replacement evidence.\u8232 Watch item: test in output-specificity later.\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa280\partightenfactor0

\f2\b\fs28 \cf0 Tone calibration\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa240\partightenfactor0

\f0\b0\fs24 \cf0 Current baseline status: partial.\uc0\u8232 Key risk: one-size-fits-all tone advice.\u8232 Recommendation IDs: R04.\u8232 Revision scope note: tie tone to supplied brief, copy, product, situation or observable cues.\u8232 Watch item: no invented brand tone in baseline/no-brief mode.\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa280\partightenfactor0

\f2\b\fs28 \cf0 Copy handling\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa240\partightenfactor0

\f0\b0\fs24 \cf0 Current baseline status: partial.\uc0\u8232 Key risk: \'93clear delivery\'94 without line, cue-word or message evidence.\u8232 Recommendation IDs: R04, R20.\u8232 Revision scope note: add copy evidence anchors.\u8232 Watch item: voiceover evidence is conditional.\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa280\partightenfactor0

\f2\b\fs28 \cf0 Product / brand / situation grounding\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa240\partightenfactor0

\f0\b0\fs24 \cf0 Current baseline status: partial.\uc0\u8232 Key risk: invented brand, buyer, product or target audience claims.\u8232 Recommendation IDs: R04, R05, R17.\u8232 Revision scope note: require supplied or observable grounding.\u8232 Watch item: no-brief outputs must stay cautious.\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa280\partightenfactor0

\f2\b\fs28 \cf0 Direct-to-camera versus reader-scene handling\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa240\partightenfactor0

\f0\b0\fs24 \cf0 Current baseline status: partial.\uc0\u8232 Key risk: universal eyeline/camera rules.\u8232 Recommendation IDs: R06, R13.\u8232 Revision scope note: split direct-to-camera, off-camera-reader and scene-style handling.\u8232 Watch item: no direct-to-camera default.\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa280\partightenfactor0

\f2\b\fs28 \cf0 No-dialogue / silent-vignette Commercial\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa240\partightenfactor0

\f0\b0\fs24 \cf0 Current baseline status: non-compliant / missing.\uc0\u8232 Key risk: silent reaction and non-verbal Commercial work ignored.\u8232 Recommendation IDs: R07.\u8232 Revision scope note: add conditional task-present handling.\u8232 Watch item: evidence thinner.\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa280\partightenfactor0

\f2\b\fs28 \cf0 Voiceover-style Commercial as conditional\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa240\partightenfactor0

\f0\b0\fs24 \cf0 Current baseline status: partial.\uc0\u8232 Key risk: voiceover tone lists become all-Commercial categories.\u8232 Recommendation IDs: R08, R19.\u8232 Revision scope note: conditional voiceover/spoken-copy only.\u8232 Watch item: do not collapse Commercial into Voice / Singing or VO.\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa280\partightenfactor0

\f2\b\fs28 \cf0 UGC / social-style limitation\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa240\partightenfactor0

\f0\b0\fs24 \cf0 Current baseline status: partial.\uc0\u8232 Key risk: unsupported UGC rules invented.\u8232 Recommendation IDs: R09.\u8232 Revision scope note: carry as limitation.\u8232 Watch item: no universal UGC rubric.\

\f2\b\fs28 \cf0 Presenter-led product limitation\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa240\partightenfactor0

\f0\b0\fs24 \cf0 Current baseline status: partial.\uc0\u8232 Key risk: presenter/product language overbuilt from weak evidence.\u8232 Recommendation IDs: R09.\u8232 Revision scope note: limitation only.\u8232 Watch item: future research only if needed.\

\f2\b\fs28 \cf0 Corporate / industrial limitation\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa240\partightenfactor0

\f0\b0\fs24 \cf0 Current baseline status: partial.\uc0\u8232 Key risk: corporate/industrial assumed from generic Commercial evidence.\u8232 Recommendation IDs: R09.\u8232 Revision scope note: limitation only.\u8232 Watch item: do not invent corporate criteria.\

\f2\b\fs28 \cf0 No-brief brand / product / situation invention\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa240\partightenfactor0

\f2\b\fs28 \cf0 Technical assessability versus performance\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa240\partightenfactor0

\f0\b0\fs24 \cf0 Current baseline status: partial.\uc0\u8232 Key risk: poor tape becomes poor Commercial acting.\u8232 Recommendation IDs: R10.\u8232 Revision scope note: technical limitations narrow reliability.\u8232 Watch item: preserve caps and blockers.\

\f2\b\fs28 \cf0 Audio / speech audibility\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa240\partightenfactor0

\fs28 \cf0 COMMERCIAL-AUDIT handoff summary\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa240\partightenfactor0

\f0\b0\fs24 \cf0 COMMERCIAL-AUDIT is complete. The current Commercial baseline is directionally correct because Commercial is already an operational type and the supplied baseline recognises clarity, naturalism, camera connection, copy/brand tone and technical readability. However, COMMERCIAL-SYN shows that the baseline is still too generic to be revision-ready. It does not yet strongly prevent Commercial feedback from becoming theatre-style acting feedback or generic screen acting feedback, and it does not yet provide enough observable anchors for the 
\f3\fs26 acting
\f0\fs24  field when it is used as Commercial presence / naturalism.\
The highest-priority revision need is Commercial field semantics. COMMERCIAL-REV should clarify that Commercial acting/presence means observable copy communication, grounded task-calibrated tone, camera relationship, addressee logic, product/situation grounding where supplied and believable scale. Generic language such as \'93natural\'94, \'93confident\'94, \'93strong presence\'94, \'93relatable\'94, \'93authentic\'94, \'93marketable\'94 or \'93bookable\'94 must be replaced with specific behavioural evidence.\
The second priority is claim scope. Commercial reports must not invent brand, product, buyer, target audience, campaign world or casting fit where no brief/copy/product context exists. Direct-to-camera, off-camera-reader and scene-style Commercial work need separate camera and eyeline handling. Voiceover-style evidence is conditional only. UGC/social, presenter-led product and corporate/industrial remain limitations.\
The third priority is fairness and assessability. B2 supports clear sight/sound, task-appropriate framing, controlled eyeline and simple domestic capture as assessability conditions, while B3 blocks production polish, expensive equipment, paid readers, upload/fee burden, protected-characteristic inference, nudity/stunt/privacy overreach and access needs as deficits. Technical or audio weaknesses should narrow reliability before becoming Commercial-performance criticism.\
No score fields, weights, caps, blockers, verdict thresholds, role-fit bounds, backend logic, schema, pipeline or UI changes are supported. COMMERCIAL-REV should create wording, evidence-standard and guardrail revisions only.\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa280\partightenfactor0

## Source evidence notes

### 4. Source-by-Source Evidence Notes

#### COMMERCIAL-S001 — How to Get Work in Commercials: A Beginner’s Guide

- **What the source explicitly says about Commercial as a performance or audition context:** the page states that commercials use a different skill set from stage or screen work, are shorter, often involve self-tape plus recall, and may require actors to work with a client or product in mind within a smaller character window. citeturn2view0turn11view0turn18view0
- **What it explicitly says about realism, naturalism, tone, energy or conversational scale:** it tells actors to read the whole scene, understand the tone, and focus on authenticity because brands often cast relatable people and are moving away from “put on” performances. citeturn11view0turn11view3
- **What it explicitly says about camera relationship, direct address, eyeline or reader/scene setup:** there is no direct camera or eyeline rule, but the page says commercial auditions usually involve acting the whole scene and that recall may add the other character, which means scene relationship may matter later in process. citeturn11view0
- **What it explicitly says about copy, product, brand, situation or audience handling:** the breakdown may specify the brand or product, narrative, treatment images, character description and commercial scenario; actors are told to use those materials as the basis for performance. citeturn3view1turn11view0
- **What it explicitly says about non-dialogue, facial/physical storytelling or silent reaction work:** commercials may have no dialogue, and actors may still need to carry emotion and tone without text. citeturn11view2
- **What the source supports as tape-observable:** tone reading, authenticity, whole-scene response, handling requested props / sports / gestures where instructed, and responsiveness to supplied character narrative. citeturn11view0turn11view1
- **What the source implies is live-room-only or process-only:** paperwork, forms, travel, measurements, recall administration and opposite-character recall work belong to process rather than finished-tape scoring. citeturn11view0turn18view1
- **Any source-specific phrasing that must not be universalised / any criteria that should not become scoring criteria:** “client involved”, “target audience”, “specific idea in mind”, luck, measurements, right-to-work and other admin/form details must not be turned into performance criteria. citeturn18view0turn18view1
- **Extraction limitation:** the page is broad, introductory and partly process-facing; it helps define Commercial context, but it is not a formal assessment framework. citeturn2view0turn11view0

#### COMMERCIAL-S004 — 19 Tips to Nail Your Commercial Audition

- **What the source explicitly says about Commercial as a performance or audition context:** it treats Commercial auditions as a copy- and circumstance-led form where actors need to put their own stamp on the material without drifting away from the spot’s style. citeturn12view2
- **What it explicitly says about realism, naturalism, tone, energy or conversational scale:** “appropriate realism” is presented as central; actors should speak as they do in real life, understand the style and tone of the spot, and make the copy lively and natural rather than stiff. citeturn5view0turn12view2
- **What it explicitly says about camera relationship, direct address, eyeline or reader/scene setup:** actors should communicate with the person behind the camera or the scene partner; eyeline depends on the spot and who is being spoken to; even the slate should feel conversational and relaxed. citeturn12view0turn12view1
- **What it explicitly says about copy, product, brand, situation or audience handling:** the article says to research the brand, find the right pacing for 15–30 second spots, and bring yourself to little-copy scenarios through internal dialogue and lived circumstances. citeturn12view2turn12view0
- **What it explicitly says about non-dialogue, facial/physical storytelling or silent reaction work:** little-copy spots still require embodied inner life; prop interaction is suggested as a way to ground relationships and world. citeturn12view2turn3view7
- **What the source supports as tape-observable:** realism, tone match, eyeline choice, pacing, prop relationship, internal life in little-copy work and relaxed slate address. citeturn12view0turn12view2
- **What the source implies is live-room-only or process-only:** sending prop/no-prop options and taking acting or improv classes are process suggestions, not direct scoring evidence. citeturn3view7turn12view1
- **Any source-specific phrasing that must not be universalised / any criteria that should not become scoring criteria:** “you are the product”, archetype shorthand, memorable “button”, personality language, prop preference and improv advice are all too coach-shaped to become direct criteria. citeturn12view2turn12view3
- **Extraction limitation:** strong for descriptor language, weak for universality. citeturn12view2

- **What the source implies is live-room-only or process-only:** its callback / booking language is outcome-based and not safe tape evidence. citeturn15view1

- **Extraction limitation:** useful for direct-to-camera motivation, but highly coach-shaped. citeturn13view0

#### COMMERCIAL-S007 — Commercial Audition Basics From Casting Director Laurie Records

- **What the source explicitly says about Commercial as a performance or audition context:** it says commercial auditions should never be expected to work like film / TV auditions and calls the difference “apples and oranges”. citeturn4view7turn13view2

- **What it explicitly says about camera relationship, direct address, eyeline or reader/scene setup:** it states that LA commercial auditions often place the copy on a cue card just off camera, which makes off-camera copy-reading a commercial-specific skill. citeturn14view0
- **What it explicitly says about copy, product, brand, situation or audience handling:** if the copy is unclear, ask; a wrong commercial choice can waste a take, and commercial copy may require different preparation from theatrical sides. citeturn13view2turn14view0
- **What it explicitly says about non-dialogue, facial/physical storytelling or silent reaction work:** nothing substantive. citeturn13view2turn14view0

- **What the source implies is live-room-only or process-only:** same-day and overnight turnaround, wardrobe, headshot norms, and fast in-and-out room timing are mostly process conditions rather than finished-tape criteria. citeturn4view7turn13view2turn14view0
- **Any source-specific phrasing that must not be universalised / any criteria that should not become scoring criteria:** literal costume advice, “go straight to set” thinking, one-headshot-in-the-car advice and geography-specific cue-card customs must not become universal scoring rules. citeturn13view2turn14view0
- **Extraction limitation:** invaluable for Commercial distinctiveness and copy process, but it blends process and performance heavily. citeturn13view2turn14view0

B1 evidence is strongest where the current Commercial branch most needs it: mainstream Commercial distinctiveness, grounded realism, tone calibration, copy handling, direct-to-camera relationship, quick-turn audition context and silent-vignette awareness. S001, S004, S007 and S008 repeatedly push Commercial away from generic theatre-acting or generic “strong presence” language and toward believable, context-led choices. citeturn11view0turn12view2turn13view2turn14view1

**Direct-to-camera commercial evidence** is solid enough to proceed: S004 covers eyeline and address relative to spot structure, S005 is explicitly about solo spoken-to-camera commercials, and S007 adds the off-camera cue-card convention that often shapes Commercial delivery. citeturn12view0turn13view0turn14view0

**Scene-style commercial evidence** exists but is thinner. S001 talks about whole-scene acting, scenario reading and recall with another character; S004 says eyeline depends on who is being addressed and whether there is a person behind the camera or a scene partner. That is enough to stop a false direct-to-camera default, but not enough to build a rich scene-style subtype alone. citeturn11view0turn12view0

**No-dialogue commercial evidence** is meaningful but concentrated. S001 confirms that commercials often work without dialogue, and S006 gives the batch’s clearest account of silent reaction, facial/body variation and product-world imagination. The subtype is therefore present, but much of its detail is coach-shaped. citeturn11view2turn15view2turn15view3

**Copy / product / brand / situation evidence** is one of B1’s strongest areas. S001, S004, S007 and S008 all tie performance choices to the supplied brand, product, campaign, script, treatment or scenario rather than general acting instinct alone. citeturn3view1turn12view2turn14view0turn14view1

B1 evidence remains thin for **UGC / social-style**, **presenter-led product work**, **corporate / industrial**, and **voiceover-style Commercial** contexts. None of the eight extracted pages gives stable descriptor language for those areas, and S007 only mentions web content and industrials in Laurie Records’ biography, not as auditable assessment guidance. This should stay a limitation for later B4 or a final limitation register rather than being overbuilt now. citeturn14view0turn16view0turn11view0turn12view2

The **theatre-acting leakage risk** is clearly evidenced in B1. Commercials are repeatedly described as unlike theatrical auditions, and overplaying, generic “big” screen work or punched-comedy selling are actively discouraged. citeturn2view0turn12view0turn4view7turn16view0

The **marketability / appearance / bookability exclusion** is not formally solved by B1. What B1 does show is that the usable performance evidence clusters around realism, tone, context, copy and camera relationship rather than social profile or marketability talk. Formal exclusion still belongs to B3. citeturn11view0turn12view2turn14view0turn14view1

The **no-brief brand/product invention caution** is moderately supported already: B1 repeatedly tells actors to work from the breakdown, treatment, campaign history, script clues or clarifying questions, not from guessed commercial worlds. citeturn11view0turn14view0turn6view6

### 11. B3 Readiness and Extraction Order Check

The original extraction order **B1 → B3 → B2 → B4 conditional** still holds.

B1 confirms that **B3 should remain next** because the batch now establishes what mainstream Commercial performance broadly looks like, but it also exposes exactly where later overclaim risk sits: target-audience talk, “you are the product” shorthand, wardrobe literalism, coach methods, and campaign-specific taste language. Those need official process, fairness, access and anti-bias bounding before B2 execution detail is layered on top. citeturn18view0turn12view2turn13view2turn14view1

No B1 gap is strong enough to justify moving **B2 ahead of B3**. B1 already surfaced some execution detail — eyeline, cue cards, slate tone, props, self-tape curation — but the bigger immediate risk is not missing technique language; it is overclaiming, bias drift and importing coach taste before the official limits are set. citeturn12view0turn14view0turn14view1

B1 does suggest that **B4 may still be required later**, but only after B3 and B2. The current batch does not materially cover UGC/social-style, presenter-led product, corporate/industrial or voiceover-style Commercial work. That limitation can remain explicit through synthesis unless later stages find a real need for targeted gap-fill. citeturn11view0turn12view2turn14view0turn14view1

## Reusable handoff pack

### 12. Reusable Handoff Pack for COMMERCIAL-B3 and Later COMMERCIAL-SYN

#### COMMERCIAL-B1 handoff summary

COMMERCIAL-B1 is complete and has established a usable first-pass evidence base for what makes Commercial distinct from generic Acting. The strongest recurring pattern is that mainstream Commercial performance is not defined by theatre-sized acting, generic “presence”, or exaggerated salesmanship. Instead, the batch clusters around believable, relatable, grounded reality; tone calibration from the supplied brief, campaign or script clues; copy handling under fast-turnaround conditions; and camera-aware behaviour in either direct-to-camera or scene-framed setups. S001, S004, S007 and S008 do most of the heavy lifting here, with S005 strengthening direct-address handling and S006 providing the clearest no-dialogue / silent-vignette evidence. citeturn11view0turn12view2turn13view0turn13view1turn14view0turn14view1

B1 also clarifies that Commercial should not be treated as a simple extension of theatre acting or generic screen acting. Several pages explicitly contrast Commercial with theatrical or film/TV audition norms, pointing to shorter prep windows, client/product-led specificity, faster rooms, cue-card use in some markets, and the need to judge tone against the actual commercial world rather than against an actor’s default dramatic instinct. That difference is important because the current TapeCoach Commercial baseline places 60% of weight on `acting` understood as presence / naturalism. B1 now gives later stages a basis for turning that vague idea into evidence-led wording without changing architecture. citeturn18view0turn4view7turn14view0turn14view1

The main limitation is source shape. Much of B1 is platform-hosted, named-expert or coach-shaped rather than official or standards-based. S002 is especially thin as written evidence because the page is mainly a video wrapper, and S003 is only weakly Commercial-specific because it mostly covers graduate showcase and general self-tape advice. Even among the stronger pages, risky shorthand appears: “you are the product”, “who / pre-life”, wardrobe literalism, callback claims and technique packages that may help rehearsal but should not become direct scoring criteria. B1 also remains thin on UGC/social-style, presenter-led product, corporate/industrial and voiceover-style Commercial contexts. Those gaps should remain explicit limitations unless later batches produce real convergence. citeturn4view2turn7view1turn12view2turn13view0turn13view1turn14view0

Most importantly, B1 confirms that B3 should come next. The current batch establishes distinctiveness, but it does not yet provide the official fairness, access, anti-bias and claim-scope limits needed to bound risky Commercial language around client taste, relatability, wardrobe, target audience, appearance and marketability. citeturn18view0turn12view2turn14view0turn14view1

Across the B2 corpus, the most stable common denominator is legibility rather than polish: a readable frame, a workable eyeline, an off-camera reader where dialogue is involved, clear sound, simple light, and a non-distracting background recur much more consistently than any requirement for expensive gear or studio finish. Where sources become more specific about kit, editing or wardrobe, the advice usually shifts from assessability into platform or practitioner preference, and must therefore be bounded later. citeturn12view1turn4view3turn5view1turn7view1turn8view0turn9view0turn9view8

**Source-by-Source Evidence Notes**

**COMMERCIAL-S009 — Advice for Self-Taping**

- The source treats self-tape execution as a legibility problem: quiet room, simple background, limited props, shadow-aware lighting, stable camera, off-camera reader, landscape phone capture and readable sound. It also gives a specific capture pattern of long shot into close framing. citeturn3view0turn11view0turn12view1
- Framing is explicit: begin with a long shot showing the full body, then move to a close-up just below the shoulders, keep the frame tight through the take, avoid multiple angles and profile-heavy shooting, and do not show the reader. citeturn11view0turn12view1turn3view1
- Eyeline is explicit and non-universal: the performer's focus should stay with a reader positioned next to the camera rather than directly into camera; that clearly supports off-camera reader-style setup, but it must not be turned into a universal Commercial rule because B1 already established that direct-to-camera commercials exist. citeturn11view0turn12view1
- Reader guidance is strong: self-reading, leaving pauses for “imagined” dialogue and reader-app playback are discouraged because they flatten reality; any live reader is preferred. citeturn3view0turn11view0
- Tape-observable evidence includes framing, reader visibility, movement, background, sound quality, hair covering the face, front-vs-overhead lighting, logos / stripes and over-literal costume use. Process-only items include file format, password protection, public-vs-private upload, and slate content. citeturn3view0turn3view2turn12view0turn12view1
- Non-universal or later-bounded items include the English-only slate plus nationality / passport prompts, the “make it look professional” phrase, and the warning about small iPhone files for US productions. Those are not valid later scoring criteria. citeturn11view0turn12view1

**COMMERCIAL-S010 — How to Self-Tape**

- The source gives a straightforward self-tape setup recipe centred on readability: soft lighting, minimal background noise, camera at eye level, front light, plain or grey background, reader near the camera, mid-close framing and clear clip labelling. citeturn4view0turn4view3
- Framing is explicit but not absolute: the default is a mid-close shot from chest to top of head unless the request says otherwise. That makes the source useful for default readability, not for a universal Commercial frame law. citeturn4view3
- Eyeline is explicit: it should sit close to the camera so both sides of the face remain visible; direct camera address is not presented as the default performance rule here. citeturn4view3
- Audio and reader guidance are pragmatic: keep background noise down, sit close to the phone if filming on it, and keep the reader from overrunning the tape vocally. citeturn4view0turn4view3
- Slate, ident, file conversion, naming and sending are well covered, but those remain process-only rather than talent evidence. The same applies to the article’s brand, model and price suggestions. citeturn4view0turn4view3
- The article’s “nothing fancy is needed” line is useful, but it sits alongside optional spend recommendations, so the source should support assessability guardrails rather than equipment-based merit. citeturn4view0

**COMMERCIAL-S011 — Casting Directors’ Self-Tape Top Tips**

- This source is contributor-led and gives the clearest “basic readability over polish” message in the Spotlight subset: the casting team wants to see and hear the performer clearly, in a quiet space, with a readable point of focus and with sensible limits on takes. citeturn5view0turn5view1
- Framing guidance is mostly head-and-shoulders, with ident / longshot only if requested. That is useful as a default, but plainly conditional on instructions. citeturn5view1turn5view4
- Eyeline guidance is mixed and therefore cannot be universalised: one contributor says left / right of camera and not down lens, while another article passage pairs “tight eyeline” with wording that reads as profile-facing. That inconsistency itself is a caution flag. citeturn5view0turn5view1turn5view4
- Reader guidance is practical rather than stylised: the reader should be someone the actor can work freely with, not someone who corrects or blocks them. The source also treats repeated rehearsal and just a few recorded takes as preferable to endless re-taping. citeturn5view4turn5view0
- Tape-observable items are clear visibility, audibility, quiet environment, shot tightness and eye-line control. Process-only elements are instructions, labelling and delivery route. citeturn5view0turn5view6
- The main limitation is contextual: this is a young-performer / competition article whose casting contributors have also cast commercials, but the page is not a Commercial-specific standards document. citeturn2view2

**COMMERCIAL-S012 — A Beginner’s Guide to Self Tapes**

- The source is broad and actor-facing. It is useful for room sufficiency, backdrop flexibility, smartphone acceptability, reader function, close sightlines, slate basics and low-budget workarounds such as books for camera height and borrowed / shared resources. citeturn6view0turn6view1turn6view5turn6view6
- Framing evidence is broader than some of the other sources: it assumes many self-tapes need enough room for a wider or full-body shot, which is important for task-sufficient visibility in some Commercial contexts. citeturn6view0
- Eyeline guidance is explicit but general: sightlines should stay close to camera and accidental looks straight down the lens should be avoided. Reader quality matters because a loud, stiff or stumbling reader becomes a distraction rather than support. citeturn6view1turn6view5
- Audio is treated as make-or-break for assessability, but the article drifts into software-and-polish language by promoting editing and audio tools. That material is useful only as optional process support, not as talent evidence. citeturn6view2turn6view3
- Slate guidance is partially useful and partially risky: most requested slate content should come from the call, extras should not be added, and the source suggests a subtly brighter slate for commercials. That last point is clearly coach-shaped and should not become a scoring norm. citeturn6view5
- Accessibility and communication-support content is thin. The only directly relevant operational note is that Zoom can be workable if no good local reader is available. citeturn6view1

**COMMERCIAL-S013 — Master Your Self Tape: 14 Top Tips From Casting Directors**

- The strongest B2 value here is anti-overproduction language combined with a casting-director roundup: keep the background clean, use clear sound and video, focus on the performance rather than flashy edits, use a live reader and keep the take count low. citeturn7view1turn7view3turn8view0
- The source contributes little on exact shot composition or eyeline, but it helps separate performance quality from packaging. It repeatedly frames framing, wardrobe and file naming as instruction-following tasks rather than aesthetic merit. citeturn7view3turn8view0
- Reader guidance is strong and relevant: do not use a recording of yourself for the other part if a live reader can be used, because a live reader makes the interaction more natural and connected. citeturn7view0turn7view6
- The article is also unusually explicit that casting wants only a few strong takes, not many average ones. That is useful for anti-overproduction and for distinguishing “more coverage” from “better performance.” citeturn7view4
- Process-only or risky material includes submit-early rhetoric, first-impression rhetoric, explicit agent-communication rules, three-point-lighting language and external-mic suggestions. None of that should become talent scoring. citeturn7view1turn7view2turn8view0
- The limitation is source shape: it is a recent platform roundup, not a standard, and it mixes good anti-polish guidance with obvious visibility / professionalism heuristics. citeturn2view4turn8view0

**COMMERCIAL-S014 — How to Make a Perfect Self-Tape**

- This is the broadest and most detailed source in the batch. It is strongest on the distinction between readable technical quality and “professional-level” polish, on reader placement, on medium close-up default framing and on conditional slating. citeturn9view0turn9view1turn9view5turn10view2
- Framing guidance is not one-size-fits-all: the article defaults to a medium close-up for most reads, but also gives a clear example of a tape that was too tight to show how the actor lived in the body, and it recognises that some slates or requests want full-body material. That supports task-sufficient visibility rather than a single frame law. citeturn8view1turn10view2turn13view7
- Reader guidance is detailed: a live reader is preferable, the reader should not distract, reader lines must remain audible, reader accents can distract, and the most effective eyeline is with the reader almost straddling the tripod next to the camera. citeturn9view1
- The source strongly supports neutral or improvised home backgrounds and readable lighting, while also pushing optional gear. The “not necessarily professional-level quality” phrase is important because it limits how far later technical evaluation should drift toward production value. citeturn9view0turn10view0turn13view0turn13view1turn13view4
- Slate, editing and submission are especially process-forward here: slate only if instructed, slate separately, follow directions precisely, and submit electronically. Early submission may sometimes attract redirects, but that is clearly a process fact, not a finished-tape attribute. citeturn10view2turn10view3turn13view2turn13view3turn13view6
- The source’s largest limitation is scope and style: it mixes useful assessability guidance with gear shopping, flattering-colour advice, flattering-neckline advice and other packaging cues that must not become Commercial evidence. citeturn9view1turn10view0turn13view0

B2 evidence is strongest on general self-tape readability: clear sight, clear sound, uncluttered background, near-camera eyelines, sensible reader setup, controlled takes and limited production fuss. It is also strong enough to support a meaningful anti-polish stance, because multiple sources either explicitly reject flashy production or directly accept phones, home walls, improvised supports and domestic backgrounds. citeturn12view1turn4view3turn5view1turn7view3turn9view0turn10view0turn13view1

B2 evidence remains thin in exactly the areas expected at this stage: Commercial-specific assessability rules; UGC / social-style capture norms; presenter-led product framing; corporate / industrial taping norms; voiceover-style commercial capture; explicit no-brief brand / product invention clauses; and operational accessibility detail beyond the B3 layer. The batch also does not independently solve subtypes where movement, product handling or presenter logic could alter framing. Those gaps are real, but they do not block a mainstream Commercial synthesis if they are carried as explicit limitations. citeturn2view1turn2view2turn2view3turn2view4turn2view5

**B4 / SYN Readiness and Extraction Order Decision**

- **Does B2 complete the assessability / self-tape execution layer?** Yes, for mainstream Commercial self-tapes and with explicit limitations.
- **Do B1 + B3 + B2 now provide enough evidence for COMMERCIAL-SYN?** Yes, with limitations.
- **Is COMMERCIAL-B4 required?** No. It remains optional gap-fill.
- **Why?**  
  B1 already established mainstream Commercial distinctiveness. B3 already established fairness, access, burden and claim-scope boundaries. B2 now closes the missing tape-legibility layer: framing, eyeline, reader use, audibility, background / lighting readability, slate conditionality, domestic capture acceptability and anti-overproduction boundaries. The remaining gaps are subtype and nuance gaps rather than core-blocking gaps. citeturn12view1turn4view3turn5view1turn7view3turn9view0
- **Which gaps remain?**  
  - UGC / social-style Commercial — still thin  
  - Presenter-led product — still thin  
  - Corporate / industrial — still thin  
  - Voiceover-style Commercial — still thin  
  - Screen-training language — optional gap-fill only  
  - Actor-facing solo-copy preparation — optional gap-fill only
- **Which gaps can be carried into COMMERCIAL-SYN as explicit limitations?**  
  All of the above, provided synthesis is clearly scoped to mainstream Commercial self-tapes and does not overbuild unsupported subtypes.
- **Which gaps would block synthesis if not addressed?**  
  None of the remaining B4-type gaps block synthesis for the mainstream Commercial branch. They would only block synthesis if the goal were to create subtype-specific rules for UGC, presenter-led, corporate / industrial or voiceover-style Commercials right now.

## Reusable handoff pack and completion

**COMMERCIAL-B2 handoff summary**

COMMERCIAL-B2 is complete and now gives the Commercial branch its self-tape assessability and anti-polish layer. The six-source corpus is not strongly Commercial-specific, but it is strong enough to answer the operational question B2 needed to solve: what has to be visible and audible on a finished tape before later Commercial feedback is trustworthy? Across the batch, the recurring answer is legibility rather than polish. The performer should be clearly seen and heard; framing should be readable and task-appropriate; eyelines should be controlled rather than wandering; a live off-camera reader should support dialogue where relevant; backgrounds should not distract; and lighting should make the face and major expression work visible. S009, S010, S011 and S014 do most of the structural work here, with S012 strengthening wider / full-body possibility where required and S013 sharpening the “performance over production” line. citeturn12view1turn4view3turn5view1turn6view0turn7view3turn9view0turn9view5

Just as importantly, B2 materially improves anti-polish control. Several sources accept phones, home walls, improvised supports, bed sheets, borrowed spaces and other domestic capture solutions, while multiple later sources explicitly reject flashy editing or production-heavy tape making. Even the most gear-forward article still says casting is looking first for readable light and clear sound, not necessarily “professional-level” finish. This gives later stages a practical basis for separating assessability from production value and for treating technical failure as a limit on confidence before it becomes criticism of acting, speech or Commercial naturalism. citeturn3view0turn4view0turn6view5turn7view3turn9view0turn10view0turn13view4

The remaining limitations are explicit and manageable. B2 is mostly generic screen self-tape guidance, not Commercial-exclusive evidence, so it does not independently solve UGC / social-style, presenter-led product, corporate / industrial or voiceover-style subtype handling. Accessibility-operational detail is also thin here and remains primarily a B3 layer. Two source-shape cautions are especially important to preserve in synthesis: S009 contains older request-bound stale items such as nationality / passport slate prompts, and S011 contains mixed contributor language on profile / eye-line. Neither should become universal Commercial logic. Because B1 already established mainstream Commercial distinctiveness and B3 already set fairness and claim-scope limits, B2 now completes the core evidence base required for COMMERCIAL-SYN. B4 remains optional gap-fill, not a blocker. citeturn11view0turn12view1turn2view2turn5view0turn5view1turn5view4

**Compact provisional findings list**

- **COMMERCIAL-B2-F01** — Assessability is a genuine precondition for reliable Commercial feedback.
- **COMMERCIAL-B2-F02** — Framing should be task-specific rather than universal.
- **COMMERCIAL-B2-F03** — Reader-scene self-tapes default to near-camera off-lens eyelines; direct-to-camera remains request-specific.
- **COMMERCIAL-B2-F04** — Reader handling matters on tape, but reader access remains process rather than talent evidence.
- **COMMERCIAL-B2-F05** — Simple domestic capture is acceptable and does not imply lower Commercial merit.
- **COMMERCIAL-B2-F06** — B2 strongly supports anti-overproduction and performance-over-packaging handling.
- **COMMERCIAL-B2-F07** — Technical or audio weakness should narrow confidence before it becomes performance criticism.
- **COMMERCIAL-B2-F08** — Slate, file naming, upload and submission timing are process-only.
- **COMMERCIAL-B2-F09** — B2 is strong enough for synthesis once scoped by B1 distinctiveness and B3 boundaries.

**Compact unresolved-items list**

- Commercial-specific self-tape evidence remains thinner than generic self-tape evidence.
- UGC / social-style, presenter-led product, corporate / industrial and voiceover-style subtypes remain thin.
- Accessibility-operational detail remains limited in B2 and continues to depend on B3.

**4. Source-by-Source Evidence Notes**

**COMMERCIAL-S015 — Code of Best Practice for Self-Tape & Zoom Auditions for Commercials**

- Explicitly frames Commercial self-tape and Zoom auditioning as a shared process problem requiring better information, lighter burden and open communication.
- Says artists should be given relevant information when a self-tape is requested, including tone, style, period or short creative vision where possible.
- Says simplicity is key: performers should not be required to provide props or re-arrange their home as though it were a set; extras should be minor and discretionary.
- Says initial requests can ask only for a basic package such as a headshot and short slate; recall-stage additions must be reasonable, role-relevant and not excessive.
- States a reader can help but must not be an absolute requirement, and actors are not expected to pay for readers.
- Says CDs should aim for a minimum of two working days for commercial self-tapes, avoid weekends and bank holidays where possible, and use extensions or abandon the tape where the rule cannot be met.
- Says scripts needing translation should be translated for the performer unless it is only a couple of lines.
- Says artists will only be judged on performance and not on the quality of equipment available to them.
- Says actors must never be asked to self-tape fully or partially nude, nor to send nude or partially nude photographs.
- Tape-observable implication: simple rooms, limited props, absent reader and modest equipment are not valid negative talent signals.
- Process-only implication: deadlines, recall fees, pencils, extensions, translation provision and data management are not performance criteria.
- Nothing in this source should become scoring evidence about resource access, speed of turnaround, reader access or production polish. citeturn29view1turn29view2turn29view0turn29view4turn29view3

**COMMERCIAL-S016 — Equity Commercial Guides / Working in Commercials**

- Gives Commercial-specific process expectations: first audition can be in person or self-tape/Zoom; self-tape/Zoom first auditions are encouraged because they widen access and reduce time/cost burden.
- Says first casting sessions should provide the advertising agency, production company, product details, purpose of the casting and intended audience.
- States artists should not be asked for detailed personal information unless absolutely essential to the role, and should be selected on suitability rather than specific personal characteristics.
- States artists should not be asked for real age, ethnicity, pregnancy or similar details before engagement, subject to limited form and insurance contexts.
- Says the ADF and recorded materials involve personal and sensitive data, and recordings/photos from casting should be destroyed after first transmission of the commercial.
- States artists should always feel safe and comfortable in casting or shooting, and should not be asked to audition nude or semi-nude.
- Includes an equality commitment based on equal opportunity and role requirements rather than stereotypical suitability, and says advertisers should use every practicable effort to facilitate an accessible venue where disabled access is inadequate.
- Tape-observable implication: the absence of expensive travel, private studios or polished production values cannot be used as a proxy for lower merit.
- Process-only implication: recall fees, travel, ADF forms, data retention, first-audition format and safe-space rules are not performance criteria.
- This source is a rights/process guide, not a performance descriptor framework. citeturn8view0turn31view1turn31view2turn31view3turn31view4turn31view5

**COMMERCIAL-S017 — CDG Code of Conduct**

- States casting should not impose unreasonable time or monetary burden and should not unreasonably affect a performer’s availability for paid work.
- Says enough time and information should be given for requests, and asks casting professionals to be mindful of a performer’s wider circumstances.
- States casting should be aware of and discuss any access needs at the earliest opportunity.
- States performers should not be asked for unnecessary personal information and should be protected from inappropriate third-party presence without knowledge and consent.
- Includes explicit boundaries on nudity and self-tapes: performers should not be asked to perform unnecessary nudity or semi-nudity in self-tapes or auditions; performers should never be asked for fully nude self-tapes or to remove modesty garments in taped submissions.
- Limits footage use and emphasises consent, permission and clarification around who will see recorded material and how it will be stored or shared.
- Tape-observable implication: personal environment, cost constraints, privacy needs and access needs must not be treated as indicators of lesser professionalism or ability.
- Process-only implication: time burden, cost burden, consent, presence of others, permissions and access arrangements are not performance criteria.
- This source is broad and ethics-led; it must not be converted into a Commercial acting standard. citeturn7view0turn7view1turn7view2turn7view3turn7view4

**COMMERCIAL-S018 — Casting Questions Card**

- Says performers should not, in most casting, audition or interview contexts, be asked questions about age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage/civil partnership, pregnancy/maternity, race, religion or belief, sex or sexual orientation.
- States protected characteristics are covered by the Equality Act 2010 and inappropriate questioning should be reported.
- Says performers must not be asked for personal information verbally or in writing before or during the audition process, including address, personal phone numbers, ethnicity and age, except where actual age must be identified for children and age-restricted products in advertising.
- Tape-observable implication: none; this is not a tape-evidence source.
- Process-only implication: protected-characteristic handling is a fairness and lawfulness boundary, not performance evidence.
- This source must not be converted into hidden eligibility scoring. citeturn42view0turn42view3

**COMMERCIAL-S019 — Advice for Visually Impaired Actors**

- Says visually impaired actors should be asked what format and access method they prefer for scripts and audition materials.
- Recommends providing text as far in advance as possible, because it may take longer to read and familiarise.
- Says line-feeding, recordings, enlarged text and screen readers may all be relevant access methods.
- Says PDFs should generally be avoided because they are hard to adapt and screen readers often cannot access them; Word documents are preferred and font size should be adjustable.
- Says workshop or practical direction should avoid vague demonstrative terms and instead describe the task clearly.
- Says navigation support, building-entry descriptions and access-worker discussion should be addressed early.
- Tape-observable implication: assistive formats, line-feeding, access workers, enlarged text and alternative handling of text must not be treated as deficits.
- Process-only implication: navigation, venue orientation, script format and access planning are non-performance issues.
- This source is access-specific and should remain an inclusion guardrail, not a hidden criterion. citeturn28view0turn28view1turn28view2turn28view3turn28view4

**COMMERCIAL-S020 — Accessible Auditions and Self Tapes for Deaf and Disabled Talent**

- Says scripts and documentation should be sent in Word format unless otherwise requested because PDFs are inaccessible for many people.
- Says working with Deaf or hard-of-hearing talent requires the casting side to source BSL interpreters where needed.
- Says many Deaf and disabled performers need extra time to prepare, read materials and organise a personal assistant or access worker, and materials should therefore be sent as far in advance as possible for both face-to-face and self-tape auditions.
- Says if performers are asked to demonstrate skills relating to their impairment, the request must be specific and honest; vague requests for “tricks” are criticised.
- Says every invitee, disabled or not, should be asked if they have access requirements, so access becomes standard process rather than exceptional treatment.
- Gives explicit examples of access requirements: step-free access, accessible toilets, guides for visually impaired performers, fatigue-managed time slots for self-taping/Zoom recalls, lighting needs for visually impaired and Deaf people, and access-worker scheduling constraints.
- Tape-observable implication: support arrangements, lighting adaptations, timing adjustments, BSL, access workers and impairment-specific clarifications must not be interpreted as weaker talent.
- Process-only implication: childcare, fatigue, venue access, interpreter sourcing and access-worker scheduling are process questions, not performance evidence.
- This source is intentionally access-led and must not be repurposed as a performance model. citeturn27view0turn27view1turn27view2turn27view3turn27view4turn27view5

**COMMERCIAL-S021 — Code of Conduct for Auditions**

- Says artists should, where possible, receive at least 48 hours’ notice of the nature of the audition, parts being cast, who will be present, whether it will be taped or recorded, and all necessary material.
- Says managers must provide as much privacy as possible and, where reasonable and practicable, access for disabled people.
- Says artists should be given reasonable time and facilities if invited to audition for an additional part not previously notified.
- Says the number of recalls should be minimised and, if recalls accumulate, travel and out-of-pocket expenses become relevant.
- Says auditions involving nudity or semi-nudity must follow the relevant schedule.
- Says performers should not be asked for personal information as part of the audition except where law allows.
- Includes advertisement-specific clauses saying audition adverts should be as specific as possible and casting breakdowns should encourage a diverse range of artists.
- Includes a self-tape clause stating artists should be given clear direction and a realistic timeframe, and there should be timely acknowledgement of receipt.
- Tape-observable implication: lateness, recall burden, travel issues, recording notice and process friction must not be treated as talent evidence.
- Process-only implication: privacy, press attendance, travel reimbursement, timeline realism and data handling are request-side or organiser-side matters.
- This is a strong general process source, but its theatre/audition ancestry means later Commercial use must stay scoped. citeturn30view3turn18view0turn18view2turn18view4turn30view0turn30view1

**COMMERCIAL-S022 — New Rules: Commercials Auditions!**

- Exact searchable preview text confirms the source is an official SAG-AFTRA explainer for the 2022 commercial-audition rules.
- The accessible preview says the new regulations cover live, virtual and self-taped auditions and apply in-person audition principles to those formats.
- The accessible preview says that during a virtual audition producers cannot request a performer engage in a stunt or dangerous activity.
- The accessible preview says no producer may request a performer audition nude; it also indicates partial nudity may be requested only with advance notice.
- Tape-observable implication: willingness to attempt dangerous self-tape activity or to comply with intrusive nudity requests is not merit evidence.
- Process-only implication: safety permissions, nudity notice and format classification are contractual/process boundaries.
- Limitation: direct page opening was blocked in this run, so extraction is limited to exact-source preview text rather than full in-page text. citeturn22search1turn14search1turn41search1

**COMMERCIAL-S023 — 2025 Commercials Contracts Summary**

- Exact searchable preview text confirms this official SAG-AFTRA 2025 summary contains audition-related terms.
- The accessible preview says that if a performer is required to pay a fee to access breakdowns or to upload self-tapes, résumé materials or similar submissions, the casting company must provide an alternate means.
- The accessible preview says payment for translation includes virtual and self-tape auditions, and translation services must be separately agreed and paid at 50% of the session fee.
- A searchable preview also shows the summary contains an auditions section, but the blocked direct access prevented fuller extraction of that section in this run.
- Tape-observable implication: inability or refusal to pay access or upload fees, and any need for translation support, are process/cost issues rather than talent evidence.
- Process-only implication: platform-fee burden and translation arrangements are contractual terms, not performance criteria.
- Limitation: direct PDF opening was blocked, so currently extractable detail is narrower than the source likely contains. citeturn17search0turn20search0turn43search0

**COMMERCIAL-S024 — 2023 TV/Theatrical Contracts**

- The official SAG-AFTRA 2023 TV/Theatrical materials create a highly detailed self-tape and virtual-audition rule set that is not Commercial-specific but is highly relevant as adjacent US process evidence.
- The extractable summary says performers must receive breakdowns/sides/scripts at least 48 hours before a self-tape deadline, or 72 hours for minors, except where urgent casting makes that impossible.
- It caps pages at eight for a first self-tape and twelve for later callbacks.
- It says performers with disabilities may request materials in an accessible format.
- It says performers may not be required to memorise or be barred from holding sides or using a prompting device.
- It says performers may not be required to record above 720p, use non-free upload or meeting sites, or use editing software or specific equipment.
- It tightly limits slate requests to named items and bans fee-based general casting calls and preferential treatment based on payment to casting services.
- It prohibits nudity or over-revealing attire in self-tapes and virtual auditions, prohibits stunts, requires secure storage and legitimate-business-purpose access for recordings, and requires consent before public availability.
- It also requires opportunities for virtual or in-person interviews on a first-come, first-served basis with accommodations for performers with disabilities, senior performers and minors.
- Tape-observable implication: held sides, prompt devices, modest resolution, free platforms and simple equipment must not be scored negatively where these are contractually protected.
- Process-only implication: page caps, memorisation, upload sites, waiting time and storage/consent rules are not performance evidence.
- Limitation: this is a US TV/theatrical source, not a Commercial rulebook, so later use must stay explicitly adjacent and non-defining. citeturn37search1turn12search7turn41search15

**Where B3 evidence is strongest**

The strongest B3 evidence is the UK official spine from entity["organization","Equity","UK trade union"] and the entity["organization","Casting Directors' Guild","UK casting guild"], especially S015, S016, S017, S018, S019, S020 and S021. That spine is strong on clear instructions, realistic burden, no paid-reader expectation, performance-not-equipment principles, no nude self-tapes, protected-characteristic restraint, data/privacy handling and access needs as fairness issues rather than deficits. On the US side, the strongest detailed extraction came from the adjacent entity["organization","SAG-AFTRA","US performers union"] TV/theatrical materials in S024, which are rich on self-tape limits, platform/equipment rules, consent and accommodation. citeturn29view3turn31view2turn42view0turn27view3turn37search1

**Where B3 evidence remains thin and must be left to B2, B4 or synthesis limitations**

Commercial-specific UK process evidence is strong, but US Commercial-specific extractability was thinner for S022 and S023 because direct page/PDF access was blocked and the extractable exact-source previews exposed only selected clauses. That means B3 is currently strongest on UK commercial burden/access rules and on adjacent US self-tape rules, but weaker on fully detailed US Commercial-only turnaround, workload and privacy mechanics. Those gaps can be carried into synthesis as limitations unless a later stage genuinely needs more US commercial-specific contractual detail. citeturn22search1turn17search0turn43search0turn37search1

## Reusable handoff pack

**13. Reusable Handoff Pack for COMMERCIAL-B2 and Later COMMERCIAL-SYN**

**COMMERCIAL-B3 handoff summary**

COMMERCIAL-B3 is complete and now gives the Commercial branch its official process, fairness, safety, burden and accessibility boundary layer. Where B1 established what mainstream Commercial performance looks like, B3 establishes what later Commercial report language must not overclaim. The strongest sources are the UK official and professional-body materials: the Commercial self-tape code of best practice, the Equity Commercials Guide, the CDG Code of Conduct, the Casting Questions Card, the visual-impairment guide, the Deaf/disabled auditions guide and the Equity/SOLT audition code. Together, these sources converge on a clear protective spine: the request side should give enough information to ground the task; self-tape asks should stay simple and proportionate; performers should not be judged on expensive equipment; readers should not become a paid hidden requirement; nude, stunt or unsafe requests are tightly bounded; privacy, consent and data handling matter; and access needs should be addressed proactively without deficit inference. citeturn29view1turn31view2turn7view1turn42view0turn28view0turn27view3turn30view3

B3 also materially improves anti-bias control. The strongest explicit language comes from Equality Act and casting-code sources: protected characteristics should not be solicited in most casting contexts, artists should be selected on ability and the requirements of the role rather than stereotyped assumptions, and advertising has only narrow age-related exceptions. This does not produce a verbatim “no marketability / no appearance bias” clause, but it gives later stages a robust basis for suppressing unsupported language about “look”, buyer fit, casting fit, target audience, charm, class-coded polish or bookability unless the brief itself lawfully and specifically supports a narrow factual reference. citeturn42view0turn31view4turn30view1turn7view1

The main limitations are jurisdictional and source-access related. The US Commercial-specific sources were verifiable but less directly extractable in this run, so the most detailed US self-tape constraints came from the adjacent 2023 TV/Theatrical materials rather than from the Commercials summary itself. That is still useful, but it must remain clearly labelled as adjacent rather than defining Commercial identity. B3 therefore closes the fairness/boundary layer well enough for B2 to proceed next, while carrying a few explicit limitations into later synthesis. citeturn17search0turn22search1turn37search1

### 4. Source-by-Source Evidence Notes

#### COMMERCIAL-S025 — Building Confidence on Screen
- The page is a LAMDA short-course offer for professional or returning actors and frames itself around transferring stagecraft to screen, working on scripts, and developing a reliable self-taping process. citeturn2view0turn6view3
- It explicitly supports stage-to-screen adjustment, independent self-taping confidence, and general screen-craft language, but it does not mention Commercial-specific performance, product copy, brand handling, or Commercial subtype distinctions. citeturn2view0turn6view3
- It supports only very broad tape-observable language such as “effective self-tapes” and “successful screen performance”; those phrases are too generic to become Commercial criteria on their own. citeturn6view3
- Its strongest limitation is source shape: it is a dated course page with a 2023 deadline and an applications-closed notice, so it is best treated as low-confidence vocabulary support rather than current Commercial guidance. citeturn2view0

#### COMMERCIAL-S026 — Actor Refresh: Solo Preparation for the Screen Actor
- This LAMDA page is stronger than S025 on reusable solo preparation: it explicitly describes a reliable, reusable and independent solo preparation process for screen, fundamentals of self-taping, and one filmed self-tape-style scene as an example of camera acting. citeturn2view1turn6view0turn6view1
- It supports Commercial-adjacent language around solo-copy or independent preparation only in the generic sense of preparing for screen before arriving on set; it does not mention Commercial briefs, products, brands, point of view, or direct-to-camera Commercial handling. citeturn6view0turn6view2
- It supports tape-observable ideas only at a broad “camera acting / self-tape-style scene” level and is therefore not sufficient to define subtype-specific Commercial evidence. citeturn6view0turn6view2
- The source is clearly course-shaped and fee-based, so its process, method and “professional self-tape standard” language must not be imported as universal scoring logic. citeturn2view1turn6view0

#### COMMERCIAL-S027 — Working Actor Practice: intensive
- The RADA page is the thinnest B4 source for Commercial-specific use. It describes a professional workshop building agility with new material, strong creative choices, taking direction on and off camera, and techniques for auditions and self-tapes. citeturn2view2turn6view4
- That makes it relevant only as generic screen/audition vocabulary. It says nothing explicit about Commercial copy, product context, brand world, presenter-led work, UGC/social style, or voiceover-style reads. citeturn2view2turn6view4
- Nothing on the page safely supports tape-side scoring; almost all useful content is training/process language. citeturn2view2
- Its authority is institutional, but the page is promotional and course-shaped rather than evaluative, so it must remain low-confidence support only. citeturn2view2

#### COMMERCIAL-S028 — How to Analyze Voiceover Copy
- This is the strongest B4 source. Terry Berland explicitly frames standout reads as having a point of view and says the script itself contains the answers for performance choices. citeturn4view0turn9view1
- The article explicitly links performance tone to visual descriptors, written descriptions, product context, and cue words. It gives voiceover examples such as intimate reads for tight shots, upbeat reads for fast food, refined reads for luxury cars, and reassuring reads for financial services. citeturn4view0turn4view1turn9view0turn9view1
- It is most useful for voiceover-style Commercial or spoken-copy contexts where visuals or script descriptors are supplied. It does not support presenter-led, corporate/industrial, or UGC/social-style rules, and it does not give on-camera self-tape setup instructions. citeturn9view0turn9view1
- The limitation is major: it is one named casting professional’s voiceover process, so product-linked descriptors and point-of-view language must be treated as conditional, not universal. citeturn4view0turn9view3

#### COMMERCIAL-S029 — Commercial Voiceover: 10 Commercial Tones to Cultivate
- This Casting Networks article is overtly voiceover-specific. It says product type drives vocal personality and offers a list of product-linked tone families, such as calm/reassuring medical reads, dreamy sleep-aid reads, upbeat household reads, formal “professional” reads, and conversational younger-skewing reads. citeturn2view4turn5view0turn5view1turn5view2
- It therefore adds some pattern language for voiceover-style Commercials, especially product-linked tone and audience feel, but not for general on-camera Commercial acting. citeturn5view0turn5view4
- It also contains overt self-marketing language — describing your voice to align with opportunities — which is process/career advice rather than assessment evidence. citeturn5view1turn5view4
- The page itself says the list is not comprehensive, which is the clearest reason it must not become a fixed Commercial taxonomy. citeturn5view1

#### COMMERCIAL-S030 — Writing an Effective Commercial Voice Over Script
- This Voices page is a client-side chapter in an “Ultimate Guide To Hiring Voice Actors”, not an actor-scoring source. It focuses on how to write a commercial voiceover script that suits brand, message and audience. citeturn2view5turn7view1
- It does add low-confidence context for spoken-copy handling: write in a conversational voice, write for the spoken word, avoid jargon, keep paragraphs readable, match vocal direction to the script’s tone, write for a target audience, and communicate the brand/message concisely. citeturn7view0turn7view3turn7view4
- It also introduces hard-sell, medium-sell and soft-sell distinctions and a simple 30-second structure, but these are copywriting / campaign-shaping ideas, not performer-score descriptors. citeturn7view2turn7view3
- The key limitation is that the page is about helping clients and hirers shape scripts and briefs. It should only ever be used as low-confidence support for copy clarity or brief completeness, not for judging performers. citeturn2view5turn7view0

### 10. Coverage and Gap Summary

A full six of six B4 rows were completed. All six sources were extracted successfully and URL-locked. There were no inaccessible, duplicate, superseded or provenance-unclear rows. All six final statuses are best described as **gap-fill only: limited criteria found**. Three are formal course / training pages, two are Casting Networks platform articles, and one is a client-facing help guide. citeturn2view0turn2view1turn2view2turn2view3turn2view4turn2view5

B4 adds genuine value in only two areas. First, it adds **partial voiceover-style Commercial evidence**: S028 is materially useful because it ties performance choices to supplied visual descriptors, written descriptions, product context, cue words and a clear point of view. S029 adds a looser product-linked tone vocabulary. S030, while not an actor-assessment source, helps explain why some spoken-copy tasks favour conversational, concise, audience-aware wording. citeturn4view0turn4view1turn9view1turn5view0turn5view1turn7view0turn7view3

Second, B4 adds **general screen-preparation vocabulary** through S025-S027: stage-to-screen transfer, independent self-taping, solo preparation, confidence on camera, taking direction on and off camera, and generic professional audition language. These pages are useful only as adjacent vocabulary support. They do not establish Commercial-specific subtype evidence. citeturn2view0turn2view1turn2view2turn6view3turn6view4

B4 remains weak or unresolved for **UGC / social-style Commercial, presenter-led product and corporate / industrial**. None of the six sources explicitly treats those as stable audition-assessment contexts. Direct address is also not materially advanced by B4. citeturn2view0turn2view1turn2view2turn2view3turn2view4turn2view5

On point-of-view and tone-family evidence, B4 helps only conditionally. S028’s point-of-view logic is the strongest narrow addition. S029’s tone families are expressly non-comprehensive and heavily practitioner-shaped. On product / brand / situation grounding, S028-S030 support grounding only when real script or product cues exist; they do **not** directly solve no-brief invention. Marketability / appearance / bookability exclusion is not materially improved by B4 and should continue to rely on B3. Cross-branch leakage risk is real: S025-S027 could bleed into generic Acting language, while S028-S030 could bleed into Voice / Singing or other spoken-delivery branches if not tightly scoped. citeturn4view0turn4view1turn5view1turn7view0turn7view3turn2view0turn2view1turn2view2
